sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: APIs play an important role in modern software development [ 8 ]. API recommendation, aiming to suggest suitable APIs for programming queries, has become a significant task in this field [ 1 , 48 ]. However, with thousands of APIs available, efficiently and accurately selecting the suitable ones is increasingly challenging [ 57 , 59 ]. Additionally, without correctly evaluating the compatibility [ 80 ] between selected APIs, it would be difficult to minimize integration errors and enhance development efficiency [ 52 ]. In recent years,

sections.text: [ 12 , 58 ]. Although existing research has made progress in generating API recommendations utilizing LLMs, these approaches have the following limitations. Firstly, the utilization of factual knowledge of APIs is insufficient. Factual knowledge refers to objective and specific information about APIs, including function descriptions, keywords, and interaction information between APIs, which are crucial for API recommendation [ 51 ]. Secondly, the impor- tance of compatibility knowledge enhancement [ 26 , 39 ] is overlooked, which fails to consider the compatibility among recommended APIs. In practice, APIs are not used in isolation, since many APIs must work together within compatibility constraints to function effectively. Moreover, the generation of recommendation reasons that align with human expectations is lacking. Those generated reasons are often uncontrollable and susceptible to hallucinations [ 27 ], with inconsistent formats that fail to consider multiple perspectives, ultimately lacking persuasiveness. Furthermore, these prompt-based methods are constrained by the limited domain-specific knowledge of LLMs, leading to poor generalization and imprecise recommendations. In this article, we propose a novel fine-tuning method, KDRAR, designed to leverage knowledge- driven reasoning for compatible and interpretable API recommendation through distillation from a teacher LLM. Specifically, KDRAR employs a dual matching strategy that matches function descriptions and keywords simultaneously. In this way, KDRAR fully utilizes the factual knowledge ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 1, Article 27. Publication date: December 2025. Unlike previous methods [ 8 , 29 , 70 ] which match user queries with similar questions from

sections.text: sets, our approach directly matches user queries with API functional descriptions. This enables the identification of the most relevant API functions based on the query, improving the relevance of the search results. Additionally, we match the keywords of user queries and APIs. We assume that there is a corresponding mapping between the keywords of user queries and API keywords. By comprehensively considering these two types of factual knowledge matching, we obtain the final candidate list of APIs to be recommended. To further enhance the recommendation process, we construct a dynamic compatibility matrix for all APIs. Each value in this matrix quantifies how frequently two APIs are used together and their level of compatibility. Since API compatibility and usage frequency may change over time, KDRAR updates the values in the compatibility matrix during inference to reflect real-time co-usage patterns. Based on the candidate API list, we extract corresponding values from the compatibility matrix and design a template that translates these values into descriptive text. This text serves as enhanced factual knowledge, aiding the LLM in understanding the compatibility of APIs while simultaneously addressing its limitations in domain-specific knowledge. Given the user query, the matched candidate API list, and the enhanced knowledge from the list, KDRAR is fine-tuned as a student LLM via distillation from a teacher LLM. First, we design specific prompts to guide the teacher LLM in generating recommendation reasons and intermediate reasoning processes for the golden API recommendation list from multiple perspectives. We make manual adjustments to the generated recommendation reasons and intermediate reasoning processes to ensure they align with human expectations while remaining consistent with the LLM’s distribution. These manual refinements also address issues such as hallucinations in the LLM’s outputs, as well as the inaccuracies in its domain knowledge [ 35 ]. Based on the aforementioned content, we construct a novel fine-tuning dataset, where the LLM inputs encompass the query, the matched candidate API list, and the enhanced knowledge among the APIs in the list. The LLM outputs include the adjusted recommendation reasons, intermediate reasoning processes, and the golden recommendation list. We evaluate the robustness of our approach across different API domains, including both Java API recommendation and Web API recommendation. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies on the proposed methods, specifically focusing on the dual matching strategy, compatibility matrix, and reasoning-enhanced recommendation to verify their contributions to performance improvements. Overall, the main contributions of this paper are as follows: — We propose KDRAR, a novel LLM-based method that leverages knowledge-driven reason- ing for compatible and interpretable API recommendation via teacher LLM distillation. This method enhances LLMs through a distilled fine-tuning strategy while considering compatibil- ity among the candidate APIs. — We propose a dual matching strategy that matches function descriptions and keywords simultaneously. This dual matching strategy optimizes the retrieval process, ensuring a more accurate alignment between the user query and API functions. — We construct a dynamic compatibility matrix to facilitate knowledge enhancement, en- abling the model to consider the compatibility and interaction among different APIs while simultaneously addressing LLMs’ limitations in domain-specific knowledge, thus improving recommendation accuracy and relevance. sections.heading: LLMs
sections.text: LLMs are complex neural networks trained on extensive datasets, enabling them to capture and simulate the complexity and diversity of human language. During the early stages of LLM develop- ment, models such as BERT [ 11 ] and GPT [ 54 ] gain significant attention. OpenAI subsequently introduces GPT-2 [ 55 ] and GPT-3 [ 4 ], which are trained with larger parameter scales and more extensive training datasets. GPT-3 marks a substantial leap in few-shot language task capabilities, demonstrating abilities beyond those of traditional pre-trained language models. Without weight adjustment and based on user-provided examples, GPT-3 excels at ICL-completing tasks. Advanced models, including ChatGPT [ 47

The development of LLMs has been characterized by the continuous increase in model sizes, exemplified by GPT-4 [ 5 ], which comprises trillions of parameters. GPT-4o [ 30 ] can process and understand multi-modal inputs, including text, images, audio, and video, making it a significant advancement in LLMs [ 24 ]. While GPT-4 and GPT-4o exhibit strong contextual understanding, they pose substantial economic challenges due to the high usage cost for many researchers. Recently, open source models such as Llama [ 63 ], Llama2 [ 64 ], and Llama3 [ 14 ] also demonstrate remarkable performance across a broad range of tasks. In our work, we utilize GPT-4 as the teacher model and Llama3 with 8 billion parameters as the student LLM. By distilling GPT-4 into Llama3-8B, we maintain state-of-the-art guidance while gaining open-source advantages: full control, reproducibility, and scalable inference. 2.2

sections.heading: Prompt Learning
sections.text: Prompt learning reduces the data format gap between pre-training and fine-tuning, enabling models to be efficiently applied to downstream tasks, often without extensive parameter training [ 6 , 40 , 66 , 81 ]. CoT prompting [ 31 , 46 , 69 ] is a technique that provides LLMs with a series of intermediate steps to derive the desired answer. On the other hand, Zero-shot learning [ 9 , 23 , 60 , 68 ] with LLMs, leverages the models’ capacity to follow instructions without requiring task-specific training. Few-shot learning [ 20 , 63 , 76 ] serves as a method for facilitating ICL, which presents demonstrative examples in the prompts to guide the model toward improved performance. Kim et al. [ 31 ] propose CoT fine-tuning to improve Zero-shot and Few-shot Learning of language models. Beyond simple prompting, decoding strategies such as Self-Consistency sample multiple reason- ing paths and employ majority voting, improving answer robustness and reducing variance across tasks [ 67 ]. Tree-of-Thoughts [ 74 ] and Graph-of-Thoughts [ 3 ] generalize CoT into search processes over reasoning trees or graphs. They allow backtracking and multi-path exploration, addressing long-dependency and complex planning tasks effectively. In our work, we also adopt CoT fine-tuning, which enables LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning processes from multiple perspectives, including functionality, compatibility, and intent. This approach allows the model to derive results that are more comprehensive and reliable compared to the directly generated outputs of the LLMs. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 1, Article 27. sections.heading: API Recommendation
sections.text: Previous API recommendation research can be generally categorized into two approaches: retrieval- based [ 18 , 29 , 34 , 38 , 56 , 62 ] and learning-based methods [ 15 , 19 , 33 ]. Among retrieval-based methods, Thung et al. [ 62 ] utilize keyword matching to retrieve APIs that exactly match the keywords. Huang et al. [ 29 ] propose a retrieval-based API recommendation method called BIKER, which employs word embedding techniques to calculate similarity scores between textual descriptions. Wei et al. [ 70 ] introduce CLEAR, an approach that leverages contrastive learning to fine-tune a BERT-based embedding model, enabling API retrieval by measuring the semantic similarity between Stack Overflow [ 2 ] discussions and user queries. However, these retrieval-based methods are limited by the representational capabilities of the embedding models and cannot deeply understand the specific requirements and queries of developers. Among learning-based methods, Gu et al. [ 19 ] use an RNN encoder-decoder model to encode a given query into a fixed-length context vector and generate an API sequence based on this vector. Eberhart et al. [ 15 ] introduce ZaCQ to better capture user intent. However, these learning-based methods are constrained by the insufficient training data in the domain, making it difficult for the current training data to cover all APIs. The rapid advancement of LLMs has created new opportunities in the domain of API recommen- dation systems [ 25 ]. Huang et al. [ 28 ] leverage a Knowledge Graph [ 21 , 50 ] guided LLM to clarify queries for API recommendation. Ma et al. [ 45 ] propose a compositional API recommendation approach for better aligning coarse-grained requirements with fine-grained APIs. Chen et al. [ 8 ] utilize LLMs to generate API recommendation lists based on enhanced ICL [ 12 , 58 ]. Although exist- ing research has made progress in generating API recommendation utilizing LLMs, these existing approaches suffer from critical limitations: (1) insufficient utilization of factual API knowledge and compatibility constraints, (2) lack of human-interpretable reasoning, and (3) limited domain-specific adaptation. These challenges primarily stem from the absence of domain-supervised learning, high- lighting LLMs’ inability to provide reliable recommendations without structured, task-specific guidance. In our work, we propose a novel LLM-based method that improves the effectiveness of API recommendation by incorporating structured domain knowledge and reasoning. By adopting reasoning-enhanced API recommendation, our method not only enhances the performance of the API recommendation model but also provides reasonable explanations for the recommendation results with low resource consumption, effectively addressing the limitations of previous prompting- only LLM-based methods. 3

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we propose a novel method for compatible and interpretable API recommendation called KDRAR. KDRAR fully utilizes factual knowledge from both APIs and user queries, and leverages knowledge-driven reasoning for API recommendation via teacher LLM distillation. We provide an overview of KDRAR and the problem definition of our task, followed by a detailed description in the subsequent subsections. 3.1

sections.heading: Knowledge Enhancement
sections.text: Dynamic Compatibility Matrix Construction. To effectively utilize the compatibility relationships among various APIs, we construct a dynamic compatibility matrix 퐶푀 based on the co-usage of APIs in the dataset. Figure 3 shows the illustration of the compatibility matrix. Each value in the matrix 퐶푀 represents the frequency of two APIs being used together in practice. Since API usage frequency may change over time, the values in the compatibility matrix are dynamically updated during inference to reflect real-time co-usage patterns. We provide a detailed ablation study comparing static and dynamic compatibility matrices to further demonstrate the benefit of real-time adaptation. The compatibility matrix is a key component in assessing API compatibility and improving recommendation accuracy. It is defined as a two-dimensional grid where each cell ( 푖, 푗 ) represents ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 1, Article 27. Publication date: December 2025. Knowledge-Driven Reasoning for Compatible and Interpretable API Recommendation 27:9 the number of times API 퐴 푖 and API 퐴 푗 have been used together. The purpose of constructing the dynamic compatibility matrix is to facilitate knowledge enhancement by enabling the model to consider the compatibility and interaction among different APIs. For example, when two APIs with similar functions appear, the LLM, informed by the matrix, prioritizes the API with higher co-usage frequency only when it supports accurate recommendations. This matrix identifies which APIs work effectively together and adds the LLM to recommend compatible APIs to the user. By considering APIs compatibility, the relevance of API recommendations is enhanced. For rare or previously unseen API pairs, co-usage is not the sole recommendation signal. KDRAR also considers functional compatibility and other domain knowledge learned during fine-tuning. Notably, once a rare API is correctly recommended via functional reasoning, its usage is incorporated into the dynamic matrix. This adaptive mechanism significantly improves recommendation robustness, demonstrating a key advantage over a static co-occurrence-based matrix. Knowledge Translation. After retrieving the candidate list, we query the values between the APIs in the list from the compatibility matrix, where each value reflects the co-usage frequency of a pair of APIs. Since LLMs operate primarily on natural language inputs, each raw value fails to reflect the semantic description of actual compatibility between APIs and cannot be directly consumed by LLMs as input. To address this, we design a translation mechanism that converts the compatibility signals into descriptive textual knowledge. For each API pair ( 퐴 푖 ,퐴 푗 ) in the candidate list, we generate a corresponding natural language statement using a predefined template, such as: “

sections.heading: Fine-Tuning Dataset Construction
sections.text: This phase aims to leverage a teacher LLM to construct the fine-tuning dataset used in the fine- tuning process. We design a specific prompt using CoT reasoning strategy, which combines the following components: CoT reasoning strategy instruction, user query, golden recommendation list, matched candidate API list, and corresponding enhanced knowledge. Figure 4 shows the details of the prompt for fine-tuning dataset construction. The specific prompt is employed to guide the teacher LLM in generating recommendation reasons and intermediate reasoning processes from multiple perspectives, such as functionality, compatibility, and intent. These reasons and processes may exhibit hallucinations or inconsistencies with domain knowledge. To address this, we manually correct and adjust these problematic outputs from multiple perspec- tives (functionality, compatibility, intent) to ensure they align with human expectations. Outputs that meet the expected standards are retained without further modification, preserving the original distribution of the LLM. This strategy ensures that the newly constructed dataset contains data that align with the distribution of the LLMs, mitigating the risk of catastrophic forgetting during the fine-tuning process. Input and Output of the Dataset. We design a specific instruction with the CoT strategy for fine-tuning. As shown in Figure 5 , we combine this instruction, user query, the matched candidate API list, and the enhanced knowledge among the APIs in the candidate list as the LLM’s input of the dataset. As shown in Figure 6 , the LLM’s output includes the adjusted recommendation reasons and intermediate reasoning processes, and the golden API recommendation list. Specifically, we complete the candidate list of LLM’s input based on the golden API recommendation list, replacing the lower-ranked APIs in the candidate list with the APIs in golden recommendation list that were not retrieved. sections.heading: API Recommendation Inference
sections.text: This phase aims to utilize the fine-tuned LLM to generate high-quality API recommendations. First, when given a query, we employ a dual matching strategy to obtain a list of candidate APIs from the API set. These candidate APIs are then matched with the compatibility matrix to generate enhanced knowledge describing the compatible frequencies between the APIs. Then, we feed the prompt used during the fine-tuning process, combined with the user query, candidate API list, and enhanced knowledge into the fine-tuned model. sections.heading: Implementation Details
sections.text: To gather factual knowledge of APIs, we establish a Java API dictionary with 30,287 method description pairs. The dictionary is built by parsing the JDK 1.8 API reference documentation and extracting all API methods from the HTML file of each class. We fine-tune the CodeBERT base model to our adapted downstream task with 10 epochs. For each epoch, we set the batch size to 16 and use the entire set of our constructed dataset based on user queries and API functional descriptions. For Equation ( 7 ), the parameters 훼 and 훽 are set to 0.7 and 0.3 based on ablation experiments. For API retrieval, we set the number of retrieved APIs to 5 based on extensive experiments. For keyword extraction, we utilize the GPT-4 in our paper for all experiments. We employ GPT-4 as a teacher LLM and Llama3-8B as a student LLM. While GPT-4o offers advanced capabilities, we choose GPT-4 as the teacher LLM for its ability to generate high-quality explanations at a substantially lower computational cost, ensuring a balance between efficiency and effectiveness. The teacher LLM is used to construct training data for KDRAR. For GPT-4 utilized in all experiments, we set the temperature to 0 to maintain consistency. For SFT, we fine-tune the Llama3-8B LLM with 5 epochs using the QLoRA technique. For each epoch, we set the batch size to 8. The QLoRA hyperparameters differ by dataset: for APIBENCH-Q and BIKER datasets, we use lora_r = 512, lora_alpha = 128, and lora_dropout = 0.1, for the PW dataset, we use lora_r = 128, lora_alpha = 32, and lora_dropout = 0.1. We conduct all the experiments on a server with four NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. For evaluation, we use the same prompt as used in SFT and set the maximum sequence length to 2048. For all API recommendation baselines, we directly use the replication packages released by the authors and other researchers. In the interest of fairness, all baseline models are configured with identical hyperparameters and designs as specified in their respective articles. 4.6

sections.heading: Human Evaluation
sections.text: Human Evaluation of Explanation Quality. To further evaluate the interpretability and explanation quality of KDRAR, we conduct a human evaluation involving multiple qualitative dimensions. We randomly select 500 reasoning outputs generated by both KDRAR and APIGen, and invite three expert annotators to independently assess each explanation. The evaluation is based on four dimensions widely adopted in explanation quality assessment: — Persuasiveness : The degree to which the explanation convincingly supports the recommended API, potentially increasing the user’s willingness to accept the recommendation. — Reasonability : The extent to which the explanation is logically sound and coherent given the user query and the proposed API. — Faithfulness : How well the explanation aligns with the actual characteristics, functionality, and usage context of the recommended API. — Overall Quality : A comprehensive judgment of the explanation’s effectiveness and usefulness from a recommendation perspective. Each dimension is rated on a 3-point Likert scale: 0 (poor), 1 (moderate), and 2 (excellent). We calculate the average scores and distribution across these dimensions for both models. As shown in Table 10 , KDRAR consistently outperforms APIGen across all evaluation dimensions. Specifically, 94.2% of KDRAR explanations are rated at least 1 in persuasiveness, 96.3% in reasonability, and 93.5% in faithfulness. Furthermore, 80.4% of KDRAR’s explanations achieve the top score (2) in overall quality, compared to only 62.1% for APIGen. These results demonstrate that the reasoning outputs of KDRAR are not only more convincing and logically coherent but also more accurately reflect the semantics and functionality of the recommended APIs. This confirms the effectiveness of our knowledge-driven reasoning framework in enhancing interpretability and user trust in API recommendations. Qualitative Analysis of Failure Cases. sections.heading: Comparison with Prior Work
sections.text: We provide a comparison of KDRAR with LLM-based and non-LLM-based API recommendation methods from three perspectives: domain knowledge utilization, interpretability , and generalizability . Domain Knowledge Utilization. Compared with non-LLM-based methods, which typically ignore the role of keywords, KDRAR explicitly leverages the latent associations between user query keywords and API keywords, in combination with functional descriptions, to retrieve a more accurate candidate API list. Relative to LLM-based baselines, most prior work also neglects keyword information as well as compatibility among APIs, thereby failing to exploit the compatibility knowledge embedded in co-usage data. Interpretability. Traditional non-LLM-based approaches only produce a ranked list of recom- mended APIs without explanations, and thus lack interpretability [ 37 ]. Among LLM-based methods, CAPIR does not provide reasonable recommendation rationales, while APIGen attempts to gen- erate explanations but often produces outputs that lack persuasiveness and logical consistency. In contrast, KDRAR is knowledge-driven: it first grounds recommendations in factual knowl- edge through functional and keyword-level matching, then incorporates compatibility knowledge ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 44, No. 1, Article 27. Publication date: December 2025. 27:26 L. Qi et al. via the dynamic compatibility matrix. By fine-tuning the student LLM with both retrieved and translated knowledge, KDRAR generates recommendation rationales from multiple perspectives (functionality, compatibility, and intent). Generalizability. Traditional non-LLM-based methods, often relying on deep learning models trained on a single dataset, have limited generalization ability and struggle to scale when the dataset grows. LLM-based baselines also do not explicitly explore scalability. In contrast, KDRAR benefits from a matching model pre-trained on multi-language code corpora (including Python, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, and Go), enabling effective retrieval beyond Java. The compatibility matrix is dynamically updated rather than static, and the student LLM, distilled from the teacher LLM, internalizes both domain knowledge and reasoning ability. These features provide strong scalability and generalizability. Experimental results, evaluated across multiple API domains (Java and Web APIs), further validate this capability. 5.2

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: While KDRAR demonstrates strong performance in generating high-quality rationales, it still has several limitations. First, although only 17.6% of LLM-generated rationales required manual correction, and most edits were minor, verification remains necessary to ensure quality. While manageable in our study, scaling this process to larger datasets could introduce additional cost and efficiency challenges. Second, the model’s robustness to noisy or ambiguous queries is limited. We analyze the datasets and found that approximately 10.3% of queries in the Java dataset and 10.8% in the PW dataset exhibit ambiguity or noise. As expected, performance on this subset is lower compared to clean queries, with a drop of 6.5% in Precision on the PW dataset. Additionally, certain components, including keyword extraction and knowledge injection, still rely on carefully designed prompts, which may introduce human bias and affect reproducibility or consistency across different datasets and application domains. Finally, while the majority of generated rationales are of high quality, a small subset exhibits issues in precision or clarity, suggesting that further refinements could improve the reasoning process and enhance recommendation reliability. 6

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Work
sections.text: In this article, our objective is to provide accurate API recommendations while generating faithful and easily understandable natural language explanations for the recommendation results. To this end, we introduce a novel fine-tuning method KDRAR designed to enhance API recommendation, which improves performance through a distilled fine-tuning strategy based on the factual knowledge among the candidate APIs. Specifically, we employ a dual matching approach that effectively utilizes factual knowledge of APIs with user queries to retrieve a list of candidate APIs. By constructing a dynamic compatibility matrix, we enrich the recommendation process with enhanced compatibility knowledge. We fine-tune our KDRAR as a student LLM with CoT strategy, enabling the model to perform step-by-step reasoning and deliver more accurate recommendations. Our experimental results demonstrated that KDRAR significantly outperforms baseline methods in both method-level and class-level API recommendation tasks. Additionally, we design experiments to thoroughly verify the generality of the proposed framework, as well as its effectiveness in improving the time and space efficiency of the sequence models. In future work, we plan to explore learning-based approaches for modeling API compatibility, enabling the system to automatically capture complex interaction patterns from data. We also aim to explore richer templates and hybrid approaches, such as combining structured and unstructured representations, to more effectively preserve compatibility semantics. In addition, we aim to investigate semi-automatic quality control strategies to reduce the manual effort required for generating high-quality reasoning and recommendation outputs.
